GRU4Rec’s original work identifies an objective limitation: averaging pairwise losses dilutes gradients when most negatives are easy. BPR-max instead uses softmax-weighted negative scores: −log Σⱼ softmax(s⁻)ⱼ σ(s⁺−s⁻ⱼ), plus negative-score regularization. The [official implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec) recommends BPR-max or cross-entropy and supports frequency-powered sampling and logQ correction for cross-entropy. This supports testing objectives before increasing GRU capacity; it does not establish which objective wins on this benchmark.

Recent evidence argues against assuming harder negatives always generalize better. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) compares random, popularity, in-batch, mixed and adaptive sampling, finding dataset-dependent accuracy/popularity tradeoffs. A [2024 paper revised in 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770) shows single-negative BPR and categorical cross-entropy are equivalent; guarantees change under sampling, so full-catalog loss arguments do not automatically transfer. [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) documents the false-negative problem, although its teacher-based approach should not be imported into this constrained experiment.

Practical inference: hold the GRU architecture fixed and compare multi-negative sampled cross-entropy against BPR-max using identical negative pools and training budgets. Then separately compare uniform sampling, a uniform/popularity mixture, and a modest fraction of model-mined negatives after warm-up. Exclude padding, targets and observed training positives; never use held-out labels for filtering. Treat hardness schedules, temperature and score regularization as validation hypotheses. Strong training margins alone cannot identify the bottleneck: select solely by pinned four-category macro validation HR@10, retaining one trained model per category and fixed seeds, splits and evaluator.
